title: Bias terms and decision boundaries
outcome: By the end, I can explain bias terms and decision boundaries using a traced example and a stated limitation.
scenario: Move a toy boundary with a bias while keeping its input weights fixed.
given: Score z=2u-v-3; predict class 1 when z>=0. InputsA=[2, 1], B=[1, 1].
All inputs and outcomes in this worked example are invented classroom data; no real model run is claimed.

steps.label: Trace input A
steps.detail: A score=4-1-3=0, so class 1 at the declared inclusive boundary.

steps.label: Read boundary
steps.detail: The boundary is v=2u-3; the bias sets its position.

explanation: The bias adds the same offset after the input contributions. It moves the dividing line without changing the weights that set the line’s orientation. Class 1 includes score zero under our stated rule. That is why B changes class when the bias rises by two: its score moves from minus two onto the included boundary.

counterfactual.prediction: A score becomes2 and B score 0; both predict class 1.
counterfactual.reason: Increasing bias by2 adds2 to every score without changing the weights.

student_task: Is B positive under the original or changed model? Point to the relevant step in the picture, then write the changed result and the rule or evidence that supports it.
teacher_answer: Originally B has score-2 and class 0; with bias-1 its score is 0 and class 1 because the boundary is inclusive. Changed-case check: A score becomes2 and B score 0; both predict class 1. Increasing bias by2 adds2 to every score without changing the weights.
project_evidence: For your Image-pattern Network Investigation, save the input, procedure, observed result and limitation of this check. Label this worked example as practice; use a different, previously unreviewed case when checking independent understanding.
limits: A linear boundary is a toy classifier rule. Raw score size does not automatically describe confidence or probability.
